name: Determining When at Least One of the Three Boolean Variables is True
description: Construct a program that determines whether at least one of the three boolean variables is True based on the inputs that it receives from the user.
code:
#Step 1: Read the user input for the value of the first boolean variable (variable a)
text = input("Enter 1 if the value of the first boolean variable (variable a) is True, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 2: Determine whether the value of the first boolean variable (variable a) is True 
if input_num == 1 :
    a = True
else:
    a = False
#Step 3: Read the user input for the value of the second boolean variable (variable b)
text = input("Enter 1 if the value of the second boolean variable (variable b) is True, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 4: Determine whether the value of the second boolean variable (variable b) is True 
if input_num == 1 :
    b = True
else:
    b = False
#Step 5: Read the user input for the value of the third boolean variable (variable c)
text = input("Enter 1 if the value of the third boolean variable (variable c) is True, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 6: Determine whether the value of the third boolean variable (variable c) is True 
if input_num == 1 :
    c = True
else:
    c = False
#Step 7: Write the boolean expression to determine whether at least one of the three boolean variables is True
result = a or b or c
#Step 8: Print the result
if result == True :
    print("Yes! At least one of the three boolean variables is True.")
else:
    print("No! None of the boolean variables are True.")

distractors.code: result = a and b and c
distractors.description: You might pick this because it looks like it combines all three boolean variables into a single check, and 'and' is a common word used when you read 'combine'. Step-by-step: this expression evaluates to True only when a is True AND b is True AND c is True. If only one or two variables are True, the expression becomes False. Using this line would therefore fail to recognize cases where just one variable is True — it demands every variable be True. There is no syntax error, so it can be tempting to think it's correct, but semantically it enforces a stricter condition than intended. Compared with the intended behavior, this line is missing the allowance for any single True to make the result True; instead it requires all three to be True.

You might choose this because & looks like an operator that combines values and some students think '&' is just another way to write 'and'. In Python, & applied to boolean values will produce a boolean result, so this line will run, but it behaves like a logical AND: it yields True only when a, b, and c are all True. That means it does not satisfy cases where only one or two variables are True. Additionally, '&' does not short-circuit like logical operators do and has different precedence rules; in more complex expressions that can lead to unexpected evaluations. Using this line therefore gives the wrong logical condition (it enforces 'all True') and can introduce subtle differences in evaluation order compared to the intended approach.

distractors.code: result = a or b and c
distractors.description: You might pick this because it contains both 'or' and 'and' and seems to involve all three variables in one expression. However, operator precedence matters: 'and' is evaluated before 'or', so this expression is interpreted as a or (b and c). That means it will be True if a is True, or if both b and c are True together. It will be False when a is False and only one of b or c is True. Using this line therefore misses cases where exactly one of b or c is True (unless a is True). There is no syntax error, so the mistake is logical: the grouping caused by precedence makes the condition different from the intended behavior.
